provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Civic: my community
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify members of their community.
The pupils should be able to explain how people live together in a community.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about our community. We have already learned about our family.

Content:
Members of my community include people like our neighbours, market traders, teachers and police officers. They are people who live near us. In our community, we live together by helping each other. For example, when Mama Ngozi needs water, we help her carry water from the well. We also share things like kerosene for cooking and play together in the compound.

Class activity:
Draw a picture of your community showing at least three members.

Evaluation questions:
List three members of your community.
How do people in your community help each other?
What would happen if people in your community did not help each other?

Summary:
A community is a group of people living in the same area who help each other.

topics.title: Civic: rights of a child
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list the basic rights of a child.
The pupils should be able to explain why rights are important.

Introduction:
We have learned about our community. Today we will learn about the rights of children in our community.

Content:
Every child has rights. These rights include the right to food, shelter, education and play. Food is important for our bodies to grow strong. Shelter is our home that keeps us safe from harmattan rain. Education helps us learn in school. Play is important for our happiness and health. These rights are protected by law in Nigeria.

Class activity:
Create a poster showing the four rights of a child using pictures.

Evaluation questions:
List four rights of a child.
Why is education important for a child?
What would happen if a child did not have enough food?

Summary:
Children have important rights that help them grow happy and healthy.

topics.title: Social: family types
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to differentiate between nuclear and extended family.
The pupils should be able to draw a simple family tree.

Introduction:
We have learned about communities. A family is a small community in our home. Today we will learn about different types of families.

Content:
There are two main types of families. The nuclear family includes parents and their children living together. For example, Papa, Mama, Tunde and Sade. The extended family includes grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins. For example, when Grandma and Grandpa live with us and our cousins visit during holidays. Both types of families love and care for each other.

Class activity:
Draw your family tree showing at least three generations.

Evaluation questions:
What is a nuclear family?
Who is in an extended family?
Draw your family.

Summary:
Families can be nuclear with parents and children or extended with more relatives.

topics.title: Social: culture
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify Nigerian foods and dresses.
The pupils should be able to explain why culture is important.

Introduction:
We have learned about families. Every family has traditions that make them special. This is called culture.

Content:
Nigerian culture includes our foods and dresses. Foods like jollof rice, eba and egusi soup are important to us. Dresses like agbada for men and iro and buba for women show our cultural identity. Culture teaches us about our history and values. During Culture Day, we wear traditional clothes and share traditional foods to celebrate our heritage.

Class activity:
Come to school dressed in traditional Nigerian attire and bring a traditional food to share.

Evaluation questions:
Name two Nigerian foods.
What is traditional Nigerian dress for women?
Why do we celebrate Culture Day?

Summary:
Our culture includes our foods, clothes and traditions that make us Nigerian.

topics.title: Security: home safety
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify dangerous objects at home.
The pupils should be able to list safety rules at home.

Introduction:
We have learned about our culture. Today we will learn how to stay safe at home.

Content:
There are dangerous objects at home that can hurt us. These include knives, matches, kerosene stove and electrical wires. Safety rules help us avoid accidents. We should never play with knives or matches. We must be careful with the kerosene stove to avoid burns. We should tell adults if we see damaged electrical wires.

Class activity:
Role-play showing how to safely use a kerosene stove.

Evaluation questions:
Name three dangerous objects at home.
What should you do if you see a damaged electrical wire?
Why is it important to follow safety rules at home?

Summary:
We must identify dangerous objects at home and follow safety rules to stay safe.

topics.title: Security: stranger danger
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list rules about strangers.
The pupils should be able to explain what to do when approached by a stranger.

Introduction:
We have learned about home safety. Now we will learn how to stay safe from strangers.

Content:
A stranger is someone we do not know. Rules about strangers include: do not follow strangers, do not accept gifts from strangers, and do not get into a stranger's car. If a stranger approaches us, we should shout loudly and tell an adult immediately. For example, if a man in a danfo offers you sweets, you should say no and run to your teacher or parents.

Class activity:
Role-play what to do when a stranger offers you a ride.

Evaluation questions:
What should you do if a stranger offers you sweets?
Why should you not follow a stranger?
What should you shout if a stranger tries to take you?

Summary:
We must never follow strangers and always tell adults if a stranger approaches us.

topics.title: Civic: national symbols
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify the Nigerian flag and national anthem.
The pupils should be able to explain how to show respect for national symbols.

Introduction:
We have learned about family and community. Nigeria is our big community. Today we will learn about our national symbols.

Content:
The Nigerian flag has green and white colours. The green represents agriculture and the white represents peace. Our national anthem is a song that praises Nigeria. We show respect for these symbols by standing still when the flag is raised and singing the anthem loudly with pride. When we see the flag, we remember to love our country.

Class activity:
Practice singing the Nigerian national anthem together as a class.

Evaluation questions:
What do the colours of the Nigerian flag represent?
How do we show respect for our national flag?
Why is the national anthem important to Nigerians?

Summary:
Our national symbols represent our country and we must show respect for them.

topics.title: Social: helping others
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify community helpers.
The pupils should be able to explain ways to help others.

Introduction:
We have learned about national symbols. Today we will learn about people who help in our community.

Content:
Community helpers are people who help us every day. These include teachers who teach us, doctors who care for us when we are sick, and farmers who grow our food. We can be helpers too by sharing our books with classmates, helping elderly people carry their loads at the market, and keeping our classroom clean. When we help others, we make our community a better place to live.

Class activity:
Draw a picture showing yourself helping someone in your community.

Evaluation questions:
Name three community helpers.
How can you help your teacher at school?
Why is it important to help others?

Summary:
Community helpers assist us daily and we can also help others to make our community better.

topics.title: Security: safety on the road
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to demonstrate how to cross the road safely.
The pupils should be able to identify common traffic signs.

Introduction:
We have learned about helping others. Today we will learn how to stay safe on the road.

Content:
Road safety is very important. When crossing the road, we must look left, look right, and look left again. We should use pedestrian crossings when available. Common traffic signs include the stop sign which means come to a complete stop, and the zebra crossing which shows where pedestrians can cross. For example, when walking to school, we must wait for the danfo to pass before crossing the road.

Class activity:
Practice crossing the road safely in the school playground.

Evaluation questions:
What are the three steps for crossing the road safely?
What does a stop sign mean?
Why should we use pedestrian crossings?

Summary:
We must follow road safety rules to prevent accidents when crossing the road.

topics.title: Revision and project
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to answer questions about values learned.
The pupils should be able to create a values chart.

Introduction:
We have learned many values this term. Today we will revise and make a project about our values.

Content:
We have learned about community, rights, family, culture, safety and helping others. A values chart shows the important things we have learned. We can draw pictures of our community, our rights, our family, traditional clothes, safety rules and helping others. This chart will help us remember all the values we have studied this term.

Class activity:
Create a values chart with drawings and sentences about what you have learned.

Evaluation questions:
What is one right of a child?
How do we show respect for our national symbols?
Name two community helpers.

Summary:
We have learned many important values that help us become good citizens.
